_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Working Lands & Industry' — the resource economy that defines the Cariboo and rural BC.

CALIBRATION — use this ladder. Trade-press journalism about forestry, ranching, mining, or agriculture should score well even when it's equipment-, market-, or operations-focused rather than policy-focused — a story about a piece of farm machinery or a mining operation update is a real fit, not a 0:
- 80-100: BC/Cariboo-specific forestry, ranching, mining, or agriculture stories (mill closures, beetle kill, BCTS, Cariboo ranchers and water rights, local mine operations, Cariboo Cattlemen events).
- 55-79: Canadian resource-economy trade journalism without a BC tie — Western Producer or Northern Miner-style coverage of farm equipment and machinery, harvest technology, livestock markets, mining operations and exploration, AgTech, forestry practices, sawmills, or labour/commodity stories in the resource sector.
- 30-54: Broader agriculture, forestry, ranching, or mining news (e.g. international resource-industry stories, general farm economics, climate impacts on working lands) with clear working-lands relevance but no Canadian/BC tie.
- 15-29: Tangential resource-sector mentions (e.g. a general business, policy, or science story that touches briefly on forestry/agriculture/mining) or local Cariboo civic news unrelated to working lands.
- 0-14: No connection to forestry, ranching, mining, or agriculture.

Strong fits include: BC and Canadian forestry journalism (mill closures, lumber markets, beetle kill, harvest operations, silviculture, BCTS, old-growth policy), ranching and livestock stories (water rights, grazing management, cattle markets, drought impact on ranches), mining and resource extraction (safety, new operations, Indigenous consultation, supply chains, exploration updates), agriculture in rural Canada (crop insurance, grain prices, farm economics, food sovereignty, farm equipment and machinery), and the technology helping these industries adapt — precision forestry, AgTech, drone surveys, IoT in agriculture, mine automation, sawmill modernization, climate adaptation on working lands. Also strong fits: labor and workforce stories in resource industries, environmental stewardship within working landscapes (not pure conservation, but how ranchers/loggers manage for sustainability), and science with direct implications for forestry, agriculture, or extractive industries. Penalise heavily (score 0–14): international geopolitical and war news with no resource-economy connection; consumer tech and gadget reviews; pure wildlife entertainment without agricultural or working-lands relevance; crime and judicial news unrelated to resource industries; financial market and stock ticker stories. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Kagi Small Web] Protecting our FLOSS commons from LLMs
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Bastian Greshake Tzovaras, Otto Richter, William Zijl, Codeberg News, Jul 24, 2026

Codeberg is a software repository site, a lot like GitHub but without the Microsoft business model. It made news this week by taking measures against AI-generated code, aka 'vide coding'. I'm not really a fan of the 'deny AI' response, but this document is reasonable and well argued, targeted against the abuses AI creates. For example: "At Codeberg, we are happy to provide free and open access to code. Just run git clone and enjoy. Unfortunately, these crawlers instead try to read every single page from Codeberg, no matter if it makes sense... These needless accesses create expensive database queries that diminish the service quality for all of us." Also, they're not trying to hunt down every instance of AI use, and will likely discourage but tolerate "side projects and experiments with little resource usage" and "specific tools and custom scripts that would be unlikely to find a community anyway, even if they were not LLM-generated."

items.title: [Atlas Obscura] Tuam Railway Station in Tuam, Ireland
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Tuam Railway Station opened in 1860 as part of the Waterford, Limerick and Western Railway, becoming one of the most important railway hubs in the west of Ireland.

Passenger services ended in 1976 as part of a nationwide rationalisation of the railway network, although freight trains continued to use the station until 1993.

Since then, the station has stood largely abandoned, with its Victorian buildings gradually falling into disrepair. Despite this, many original features—including the distinctive wrought-iron lattice footbridge, platform canopies, goods facilities, and water tower—still survive, making Tuam one of Ireland's most complete surviving historic railway stations.

There have been proposals to restore the railway as part of the Western Rail Corridor, but the station remains closed today.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Ancient ape fossil in Egypt challenges the story of human origins
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

A newly identified fossil ape from northern Egypt is reshaping ideas about where the ancestors of modern apes first emerged. Analyses place it closer to living apes than any known East African species of the same age, pointing to North Africa and the Middle East as a possible birthplace and crossroads for the ape lineage that eventually produced gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and humans.

items.title: [Kagi Small Web] Night owls and early birds
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

As young kids, most of us were up at 6 am, raring to go on weekend mornings. As teenagers, many of us slept in until late morning or noon. But people are different. Some love Marmite, some hate it. As adults, we start finding what works best for us. And it’s not necessarily the same as, or what works best for, our partners.

It struck me that I know a lot of couples, us included, who are night-owl/early-bird combos.

One of the couple naturally wakes at dawn and tiptoes out of bed. They’ve usually managed a host of morning peaceful time, exercise or chores before the night owl surfaces, often bleary-eyed.

And while the early bird crashes out in the evening, maybe falling asleep on the sofa, the night owl is often just getting going, hitting their productive stride, staying out, or watching late-night TV, before tiptoeing into bed next to the sleeping early bird.

Of course, we notice and talk about the differences. So perhaps there are a host of early-bird couples and night-owl couples. But eventually we all settle into the rhythms that work best for us, and I’m pretty sure I see a lot of opposites.

I can’t help wishing I were naturally an early bird on the same schedule as my wife. But perhaps it’s a combo that creates time for both partners and secretly a recipe for success?

As Kahlil Gibran wrote in The Prophet:

"And stand together yet not too near together:

  For the pillars of the temple stand apart,

  And the oak tree and the cypress grow not in each other's shadow."

Are you a night owl living with an early bird, or vice versa? How do you make it work for you?

items.title: [Atlas Obscura] The Afro-Antillean Museum in Panama City, Panama
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

During the construction of the Panama Canal hundreds of thousands of workers were imported from Jamaica and other Caribbean islands and were settled in tenement housing on the outskirts of Panama City.

Each house was constructed as small as possible, often no more than a wooden shack raised on posts to keep the insects out, with communal bathrooms and a zinc roof. It was in one of these tenement neighbourhoods, known then as Guachapalí, today as El Marañón, that canal workers constructed the Cristian Mission Chapel in their off hours, from 1909-1910.

Countless church services, weddings, funerals and baptisms were performed there, and those worshiping inside would have experienced and withstood the post-canal deportation schemes, denials of citizenship, and attempts at cultural erasure imposed on their community, as well as the eventual governmental recognition of their rights and way of life.

items.title: [Atlas Obscura] The Electrical Box Theatre in Los Angeles, California
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

On the corner of Traction Avenue and 4th Place in Los Angeles’s Arts District sits a gray utility box. Big deal, right?

Actually, yes.

Measuring roughly six feet tall and three feet deep, the city street cabinet is not that at all, even in the slightest—it’s the creation of Downtown LA artist S.C. Mero, and it’s (not literally, but still) electric.

Welcome to the home of the Electrical Box Theatre, possibly the smallest performance space in all of Los Angeles, if not the world. No tickets, seats, nor guest lists. The show starts when the door opens.

By day, it’s a forgotten piece of urban nothing; at night, with its door open to a typically unsuspecting audience, the box becomes a hub for artists and performers, and all the street’s a stage.

“Not to be corny,” Mero says, “but you just don’t know what’s in something unless you look inside it. A person, or even ourselves. I think there’s kind of a beautiful message in that.”

Inside, the theater’s lined with velvet wallpaper and theatrical details, including a clock and photos of the theater itself (even a fake utility box in Los Angeles needs headshots).

Mero is known for public art that transforms overlooked parts of the city into moments of surprise. Some of it’s impossible to miss (like a 13-foot tall mailbox); others, like the Electrical Box Theatre, reward curiosity.

Since opening, it has hosted neighborhood musicians, a clown, a mime, burlesque performances, and even a vampire with a banjo. Performers coordinate with Mero in advance and receive access instructions on the day of their show.

At its street-smart historic corner, the theater also takes a bow to the Arts District’s storied lineage of art and artists, who have long called this block home before slowly getting pushed out by the churn of city real estate reality.

And that’s part of the magic: how temporary it all feels, and the discovery that lives therein. Claiming a piece of the city back for the people, Mero has devoted this patch of sidewalk to the artists who make all things beautiful last.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover the hidden brain switch that assigns bees their jobs
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Researchers found that specific brain circuits help decide which jobs bees perform as they age. When those circuits were switched off, older worker bees began caring for the queen again instead of carrying out their normal later-life duties. The findings reveal that a bee colony’s complex division of labor may be guided by neural switches hidden inside each bee’s brain.

items.title: [Animikii News River] "AI moves fast. Human hearts move slow."
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

News River Express

News River Express is back with three articles worth your time, plus a bit of our own news.

We built this summer format so we can spend more time outside with our plants and our people, and still get the best links to your inbox.

This week is the topic everyone is talking about: AI, and where it meets Indigenous Data Sovereignty.

How Indigenous technologists are building data sovereignty into AI

BetaKit

Our CEO and Co-Founder Jeff Ward spoke at Mila's Indigenous AI Gathering in Montréal. The line that stayed with him came from Canada's Minister of AI and Digital Innovation, Evan Solomon:

"AI moves fast. Human hearts move slow."

The Minister came to an Indigenous-led space to present and to listen, weeks after Canada's national AI strategy launched. That's where trust starts, and it's how we build at Animikii: technology made with love starts with human hearts and lets love set the pace.

The BetaKit piece covers some of the conversations. Participants in the Indigenous Pathfinders in AI program pitched tools that keep data inside the community network. Diné geneticist Krystal Tsosie put the stakes plainly:

"[Data] determines what the system sees, what it optimizes for, who benefits, and who is harmed. Our community's data is already on this pathway, and the question is whether or not our community governs what it becomes."

Data centers are booming. Indigenous leaders want help protecting their lands.

Grist

AI infrastructure is hungry for land, energy, and water, and Indigenous delegates took that to the UN's Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. A single hyperscale data centre can draw as much electricity as 100,000 households. Delegates called for free, prior, and informed consent, and some US tribes have passed outright moratoriums. As Sámi Parliament member Maren Storslett said:

"We must not only ask what AI can do, but what it should do."

Respecting First Nations knowledge on Wikimedia platforms

Wikimedia Australia

Wikimedia Australia and the Indigenous-owned firm Terri Janke and Company have released a guide for handling Indigenous knowledge across Wikipedia, Commons, and Wikidata. It matters for AI because Wikimedia trains many large language models, so errors and colonial framing scale with them. The guide uses a risk-assessment approach built on one question: who has the cultural authority to tell this story? As Terri Janke and Company's Shevaun Wright puts it:

"It's not about content moderation, but about content integrity."

And in Animikii news: we are testing ethical AI with an Indigenous community

We've partnered with CEIMIA on a first practical use case for ethical AI and data governance with an Indigenous community in Canada. It pairs two tools: our Niiwin platform, and the Data Roadmap CEIMIA built for the Global Partnership on AI.

Most talk about responsible AI stays at the level of principles. This pilot asks what those principles look like when a community runs them on its own data, with tools it controls. Niiwin carries OCAP®, CARE, and UNDRIP principles into how the system behaves. Testing CEIMIA's roadmap on Indigenous data should push the tool somewhere more inclusive, because community data raises questions government data never does.

It's a small, concrete pilot to help answer a bigger question: can these systems advance Indigenous rights, not just avoid harming them? That's what we're setting out to test. More information on that pilot here.

Want to talk it through? Book an AI conversation and Niiwin demo direct with our CEO Jeff: grab a time.
